newsitem.title: USA: Group calls for market approach to future Mexicos.
newsitem.headline: Group calls for market approach to future Mexicos.

text.p: Future financial crises in emerging markets should be resolved with a market-based approach rather than by resorting to massive international bailouts, a financiers group said.

In a report to be published Friday, the International Institute of Finance also advocated that emerging economies act swiftly to adjust fiscal and monetary policies at the onset of a financial crisis.
But it saw a key role for markets, noting that falling equity prices tend to attract bargain hunters and encourage other investors to ride out the storm.

"Markets can't depend on official bailouts," said Charles Dallara, the group's managing director, at a briefing which coincided with the start of events associated with the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
"Investors won't learn the lessons they need to learn," said Dallara whose group's membership includes commercial banks, securities firms, fund managers and insurance companies.

The Mexican peso crisis of 1994/95, which prompted large-scale official assistance, has prompted both the public and private sectors to develop a range of proposals for new ways to address future financial crises should they arise.

The IIF said its proposed strategy takes into account the greater role that equity plays in emerging capital markets. The share of long-term bank claims in total debt is much lower than in the 1980s, the group also noted.
As a result, attempts to control outflows by rescheduling debt are likely to prove more difficult than in the past.
The private sector is expected to invest some $225 billion in emerging market economies this year, according to the group's chief economist, William Cline, who led the group that produced the report.

The report calls for crises to be dealt with on a case-by-case basis, rather than through predetermined arrangements supervised by official international organizations. It also rejected any approach that would create new international bankruptcy mechanisms.

But the group did call for preemptive measures to help avert potential crises. "Structural weaknesses must be addressed with persistence or they will resurface during periods of stress," the report said.

Shoring up domestic banking systems should be a top priority for emerging economies and multilateral agencies, the report said. It noted the potential for a weak banking system to "transform a temporary external shock into a sustained recession."
